To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
higher levels of hostility at college and change in levels of hostility from college to early adulthood predict increased risk for a wide range of health-related risk indicators later in midlife.
high hostility in college and changes in hostility from college into midlife are associated with increased odds for high health-related risk.

higher college hostility predicts a full range (smoking, drinking, social isolation, lower social support, low income, obesity, avoidance of physical activity, high fat diet, risk for depression) of health-related risks later in midlife, and change in hostility (declines in hostility from college are protective, while gains are risk enhancing) is related to increased health risk.

the role of hostility in health-related outcomes.
the role of hostility and hostility reduction in health.
the development of hostility, and the impact of this personality trait on physical health and well-being.

high college hostility and changes in hostility from college are related to increased health risks.
high levels of hostility at college and change in levels of hostility from college to middle adulthood predict a full range of risk indicators for health problems in middle adulthood.
hostility measured in college predicts a range of high risk indicators at midlife and that changes in hostility from college through midlife are associated with a full range of risk indicators.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high levels of hostility in college and changes in hostility from college through midlife are associated with a full range of risk indicators.
high levels of hostility in college are associated with high-risk behaviors and a high-risk status later in life.

the earlier we can identify those at high risk and help them change their behavior, the more likely we are to prevent the development of disease.
hostility is a modifiable risk factor.
